newsitem.title: USA: US retail sales data shrink chance of rate hike.
newsitem.headline: US retail sales data shrink chance of rate hike.

text.p: U.S. retail sales figures for May and revised data for April have diminished the likelihood of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in July, analysts said.
The Commerce Department reported Thursday that retail sales slipped 0.1 percent in May, contrary to expectations for a 0.4 percent rise.
Reinforcing the weak picture, Commerce also revised the April decline in retail sales to a sharp 0.9 percent, three times the size of the 0.3 percent drop originally reported.
Excluding auto sales, retail sales slipped 0.1 percent in May, contrary to a forecast for a modest 0.3 percent rise. In April, retail sales excluding autos dropped 0.5 percent.
Bond prices, which have gained recently on the view that upcoming economic data would be friendly toward the credit markets, rose after the Commerce Department report.
The benchmark 30-year bond, which was up more than a quarter of a point in early dealings, aided by a strong dollar, climbed as high as 98-8/32, up a full point, before trimming its gains.
Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, called the retail sales drop a "very important number" for the market, showing "very slow" growth.
With regard to the chance of a Fed rate hike in July, Alexy said, "This is likely to take the Fed out of the picture ... There is no persisting demand here."

William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds, concurred. "What you have is three contractions in a row," he said. "(These data) certainly call into question the underlying vigor (of the consumer and his) willingness to spend."
In addition to the declines recorded in April and May, retail sales fell 0.3 percent in March and were flat when auto transactions were excluded.
"Consumption was very soft in the second quarter, well below the 5.7 percent (rise) we saw in the first quarter," said Joseph Dziwara, economist at Sakura Bank.
Dziwara said for the second quarter, consumption would rise by only 1.0 percent.
"That means there's no way the Federal Reserve will move (to raise interest rates) in July," he said.

"The retail sales data were weaker than expected," agreed Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "They confirm and strengthen the notion that consumer spending in particular and the economy as a whole slowed quite sharply in the second quarter. We'll be lucky to get 1.0 percent real personal consumption expenditure growth."
Feinman said even the Labor Department's new jobless claims data hinted at a possible cooling in the labor markets.
The government said new jobless claims rose to 339,000 in the latest week from a revised 338,000 a week earlier.
"Claims are still at low levels and it's only two weeks' data. But it may be a hint of some cooling," Feinman said.
The data reported on Thursday are sufficient to keep the Fed on hold at the July 2 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, he said.
